subject: Agriculture
title: The Tractor Revolution
description: A 60-second lesson on The Tractor Revolution.

hook.text: In 1910, farming one acre of wheat took 15 hours of human labor. By 1960, it took under two.

buildup.text: Steam tractors appeared in the 1880s, but gasoline tractors in the 1910s made them practical for farms.

discovery.text: Tractors replaced horses and mules. A single tractor did the work of twelve animals.

twist.text: Horses ate 25% of a farm's grain output. Eliminating them freed millions of acres for human food.

climax.text: By 1960, horses had virtually vanished from American farms. The tractor had won completely.

punchline.text: The tractor didn't just replace the horse. It freed the land.

quiz.question: What percentage of a farm's output did horses consume as feed?

details.summary: The tractor revolution replaced animal power with engines on farms, fundamentally changing the scale, speed, and economics of agriculture. This topic covers the transition from horses to tractors, the social upheaval it caused, and its lasting effects on farming.
details.whyItMatters: Tractors freed one-quarter of farmland that had been used to feed draft animals, multiplied labor productivity by 10–20 times, and drove the mass rural-to-urban migration that shaped modern societies.
takeaways: In 1900, farming required one-third of US workers; by 2000, less than 2%
Replacing horses freed 25% of cropland previously used to grow animal feed
The Fordson tractor made mechanized farming affordable for small farms

faq.question: How did tractors change the economics of farming?
faq.answer: Tractors allowed one farmer to work 10–20 times more land than was possible with horses. They eliminated the need to feed draft animals, reduced labor costs, and made large-scale farming economically superior to small operations.

faq.question: What social changes did the tractor revolution cause?
faq.answer: As tractors replaced labor, millions of farm workers became unnecessary. This drove massive rural-to-urban migration, shrank the farming population from 30% to under 2% of the workforce, and fueled industrial growth in cities.
